meta.title: Flex Ltd — Revathi Advaithi's diversified EMS pivot toward AI data centre power and infrastructure assembly
meta.abstract: Flex Ltd is a Singapore-headquartered electronics manufacturing services (EMS) and supply chain solutions company listed on the NASDAQ under the ticker FLEX. The company traces its origins to 1969 when Flextronics International was founded; the modern Flex organisation reflects multi-decade strategic evolution including the November 2015 corporate rebrand from Flextronics to Flex Ltd. The company operates three reporting segments: Flex Agility Solutions (FAS, covering consumer, communications, and lifestyle product categories), Flex Reliability Solutions (FRS, covering automotive, health solutions, and industrial categories), and Nextracker (the solar tracker business that was spun off via IPO in February 2023, with Flex completing the full separation by January 2024). Under CEO Revathi Advaithi (since February 2019, succeeding Mike McNamara), the strategic mandate has been the higher-margin product and customer category emphasis, the Nextracker separation completion, and the broader strategic posture refinement toward the AI data centre infrastructure assembly opportunity plus the broader high-mix high-complexity manufacturing positioning. The fiscal 2024 revenue was approximately $26.4 billion reflecting the broader multi-segment scaling combined with the Nextracker separation impact; the fiscal 2025 revenue was approximately $25.8 billion reflecting the continued multi-segment trajectory. The AI data centre infrastructure assembly opportunity has emerged as a meaningful incremental growth driver within the Flex Reliability Solutions segment scaling.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
After the January 2, 2024 distribution of Flex's remaining Nextracker stake, Flex Ltd entered the frozen window as a cleaner manufacturing-and-infrastructure franchise, though not the outright largest U.S.-listed EMS company by revenue: Flex reported fiscal 2026 net sales of $27.914 billion, while Jabil reported $29.8 billion for fiscal 2025. Flex remained incorporated in Singapore, operationally centered in Austin, and led by Revathi Advaithi, who had been appointed chief executive on February 11, 2019. On May 5, 2026, the board approved the next portfolio break-up as well: a planned spin-off of the Cloud and Power Infrastructure business into a separate public company targeted for the first quarter of calendar 2027. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Flex Announces Revathi Advaithi as CEO](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2019/Flex-Announces-Revathi-Advaithi-as-CEO/default.aspx), [Flex Announces Intention to Spin Off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure Segment](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Intention-to-Spin-Off-its-Cloud-and-Power-Infrastructure-Segment-into-a-New-Independent-Publicly-Traded-Company/default.aspx), [Jabil Posts Fourth Quarter and Fiscal Year 2025 Results](https://investors.jabil.com/news/news-details/2025/Jabil-Posts-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/)

Advaithi's operating brief still read much as it had at the outset of her tenure: push the mix away from commoditized assembly, raise margins, make capital allocation more legible, and convert Flex's scale into stickier positions in regulated and infrastructure-heavy end markets. What changed by the snapshot date was that the strategy had been expressed in two completed or announced separations rather than one. Nextracker had already been floated and distributed; CPI had been carved into its own reportable segment and marked for exit. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Nextracker 2023 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1852131/000185213123000007/nxt-20230929.htm)

## Two Segments, Then Three

For most of the period after the Nextracker separation, Flex described the remaining company through two reporting buckets: Flex Agility Solutions, covering communications, enterprise and cloud, lifestyle, and consumer devices; and Flex Reliability Solutions, covering automotive, health solutions, and industrial. That was the structure disclosed in the fiscal 2024 annual report after the Nextracker spin. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, however, management changed the way it reported to the chief operating decision maker and created a third reportable segment, Cloud and Power Infrastructure. At the same time, FAS was renamed Integrated Technology Solutions and FRS was renamed Regulated Manufacturing Solutions. [Flex 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637424000021/flex-20240331.htm), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

The new segmentation said a good deal about where the growth had actually surfaced. ITS contained communications, high-speed networking, enterprise, satellite communications, and lifestyle categories. RMS contained industrial infrastructure, automotive compute and power electronics, and healthcare manufacturing. CPI, by contrast, was explicitly defined around Cloud and Cooling plus Power: integrated compute systems, advanced liquid cooling, and facility- and utility-level electrical infrastructure for power-dense compute workloads. By fiscal 2026, Flex's ten largest customers accounted for 45% of net sales, but no single customer accounted for more than 10%, a disclosure that underlined both diversification and the absence of a publicly named hyperscaler anchor. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## Revenue and Margin Trajectory

The financial profile across the Advaithi era reflected deliberate mix shift rather than pure volume growth:

| Fiscal Year (ending March) | Revenue | Adj. Operating Margin |
|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $30.0B | — |
| FY2024 | $26.4B | 4.8% adj. segment-equivalent margin at total-company level |
| FY2025 | $25.8B | 5.7% |
| FY2026 | $27.9B | 6.3% |

*Sources: [Flex 2025 Q4 earnings presentation](https://s202.q4cdn.com/732614612/files/doc_earnings/2025/q4/presentation/Flex_EP_FY25Q4.pdf); [Flex FY2026 results](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2026-RESULTS/default.aspx); [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)*

The peak in fiscal 2023 still included Nextracker. The fiscal 2024 and 2025 reset stripped out that solar-tracker contribution and exposed the remaining company's true revenue floor at roughly the mid-$20 billions. What mattered by the frozen date was that the rebuilt mix had begun to re-accelerate. Fiscal 2026 net sales rose 8% to $27.9 billion; adjusted operating income reached $1.764 billion; adjusted EPS rose to $3.30; and free cash flow remained above $1 billion for a second straight year at $1.060 billion. The company also disclosed its sixth consecutive quarter with adjusted operating margin at or above 6% by the March 2026 quarter. [Flex FY2026 results](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2026-RESULTS/default.aspx)

## The Data Centre Inflection

The data-centre business was the clearest quantitative expression of the mix change. In the fiscal 2025 fourth-quarter earnings presentation, Flex said data-centre revenue had reached approximately $4.8 billion and had grown about 50% year on year. By fiscal 2026, the new CPI segment generated $6.614 billion of net sales and $610 million of segment income, implying a 9.2% segment margin. Net sales in CPI rose 38% from fiscal 2025, driven by 29% growth in Cloud and Cooling and 61% growth in Power. [Flex 2025 Q4 earnings presentation](https://s202.q4cdn.com/732614612/files/doc_earnings/2025/q4/presentation/Flex_EP_FY25Q4.pdf), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

The surrounding M&A record showed how management had tried to turn that demand signal into a broader platform. Flex bought JetCool in November 2024 to add direct-to-chip liquid cooling. It completed the $325 million all-cash acquisition of Crown Technical Systems in December 2024, adding integrated power-distribution and protection systems. In May 2026 it closed the acquisition of Electrical Power Products, a U.S. critical-power specialist with more than 35 years of experience in engineered control and relay panels and modular control buildings. [Flex Acquires JetCool](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2024/Flex-Acquires-JetCool-to-Expand-Data-Center-and-Power-Portfolio/default.aspx), [Flex Completes Acquisition of Crown Technical Systems](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2024/Flex-Completes-Acquisition-of-Crown-Technical-Systems/default.aspx), [Flex Completes Acquisition of Electrical Power Products](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Completes-Acquisition-of-Electrical-Power-Products-EP/default.aspx)

That platform was no longer just a pitch deck abstraction by late 2025 and early 2026. Flex said its AI infrastructure platform could speed deployment by up to 30%; its modular rack-level CDU scaled from 600 kilowatts to 1.8 megawatts; it had deployed liquid-cooling demonstrations at Equinix's co-innovation facility; and in March 2026 it said it was already building prefabricated modular solutions for hyperscalers at a 400,000-square-foot Dallas facility purpose-built for data-centre infrastructure. [Flex announces new AI infrastructure platform to speed deployment by up to 30%](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-announces-new-AI-infrastructure-platform-to-speed-deployment-by-up-to-30/default.aspx), [Flex Expands Liquid Cooling Footprint at Equinix Co-Innovation Facility](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-Expands-Liquid-Cooling-Footprint-at-Equinix-Co-Innovation-Facility/default.aspx), [Flex Accelerates AI Factory Deployment with NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Reference Designs](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Accelerates-AI-Factory-Deployment-with-NVIDIA-Omniverse-DSX-Reference-Designs/default.aspx)

The spin announcement tied those operating facts to governance. Flex said Revathi Advaithi would become chief executive of SpinCo and serve as chairman of Flex for a transitional period; Michael Hartung would become chief executive of Flex; and SpinCo was being targeted for 65% to 75% revenue growth in fiscal 2027, accelerating to 80%+ in fiscal 2028. [Flex Announces Intention to Spin Off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure Segment](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Intention-to-Spin-Off-its-Cloud-and-Power-Infrastructure-Segment-into-a-New-Independent-Publicly-Traded-Company/default.aspx)

## The Remaining Questions

That left the central analytical question in a sharper form than the old two-segment story allowed. The historical margin work was real: ITS and RMS were what remained of the old Flex after the highest-growth infrastructure piece had been isolated. But the newest disclosure also made clear that CPI had become the fastest-growing and highest-margin reportable segment before it was even separated. The dossier therefore turned on two linked judgments. First, whether RemainCo could preserve the margin discipline that the Advaithi era had built without the CPI tailwind inside the reporting perimeter. Second, whether the infrastructure operation being spun out had enough staying power, customer stickiness, and systems-level advantage to withstand the same cycle corrections that had undone earlier EMS enthusiasms.

chapters.title: From 1969 Flextronics through 2015 rebrand, Advaithi era, Nextracker separation, AI inflection
chapters.body:
## Origins in Silicon Valley

The company that became Flex Ltd traces its origins to 1969, when a small circuit-board assembly operation opened in San Jose, California under the Flextronics name. The founding proposition was simple: take the soldering, stuffing, and testing work that technology companies needed done reliably and at scale, and do it more efficiently than in-house manufacturing teams could manage. That proposition — outsourced electronics assembly as a professional service — would underpin more than five decades of corporate evolution, punctuated by waves of acquisition, a brand reinvention, and a CEO succession that reoriented the franchise toward the higher-margin customer categories that define its present ambitions.

## The Flextronics Scaling Decades

The period between founding and the turn of the millennium was defined by acquisition and geographic expansion. Flextronics built out manufacturing capacity across Asia, Eastern Europe, and Latin America at a pace few contract manufacturers matched, assembling plants in Singapore, China, Mexico, Hungary, and Brazil into a supply chain network that could serve technology OEMs with the combination of cost arbitrage and logistics proximity their procurement organisations demanded.

By the mid-2000s, Flextronics had grown into one of the largest contract electronics manufacturers in the world. The most consequential transaction of the scaling era came in 2007, when Flextronics acquired Solectron — itself a two-time Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award winner and a former independent EMS giant — for approximately $3.6 billion. The Solectron deal added manufacturing capacity, customer relationships across the computing and networking equipment sectors, and global operational footprint in a single stroke, briefly making Flextronics one of the two or three largest electronics manufacturing services companies globally by revenue.

The financial profile through this era was characteristic of scaled EMS: high revenue, operating margins measured in single digits, intense capital requirements, and persistent competitive pressure from Foxconn, Jabil, and a tier of regionally focused Asian assemblers. The business model's fundamental tension — volume as the primary lever for cost absorption — made revenue trajectory the dominant metric and constrained the kind of sustained margin expansion that would eventually become the centrepiece of the Advaithi-era strategic programme.

## Sketch to Scale: The 2015 Rebrand

The sketch-to-scale repositioning took shape in 2015, but the legal name change came later. Flextronics International Ltd adopted the name Flex Ltd by shareholder resolution on August 24, 2016, with the change taking effect on September 7, 2016. The branding shift was more than cosmetic. It signaled a broader proposition: that Flex would engage customers from design and engineering through manufacturing, logistics, and post-sale support rather than acting purely as an assembly vendor. [Flex constitution, Exhibit 3.01](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637416000007/flex-exx301x93016.htm)

The Singapore incorporation that had been a feature of the Flextronics legal structure was preserved through the rebrand. Operational management remained anchored in the United States, a dual-geography structure maintained through the subsequent Advaithi era. The Flex Ltd name and the sketch-to-scale framing gave the commercial organisation a language for engaging customers who wanted a manufacturing partner rather than a pure vendor — a distinction that carried more weight in automotive and industrial product categories, where design cycles are longer and switching costs higher, than in consumer electronics assembly, where price-per-unit compression remained the dominant procurement dynamic.

## The Advaithi Succession

Mike McNamara had led Flextronics and then Flex through the Solectron integration, the 2008–09 global demand downturn, and the sketch-to-scale repositioning. When the board announced in February 2019 that Revathi Advaithi would succeed him as President and Chief Executive Officer, it was signalling a shift in strategic emphasis as much as a change in leadership.

Advaithi arrived from Eaton Corporation, where she had served as President and Chief Operating Officer of the Electrical Sector. Her background — a mechanical engineering degree from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science at Pilani, an MBA from the Thunderbird School of Global Management, and more than two decades of operating experience at Eaton spanning global manufacturing, supply chain, and electrical systems — was different in texture from the EMS-native career that McNamara represented. The Eaton Electrical Sector experience gave Advaithi direct familiarity with the industrial and power-infrastructure customer categories that would eventually become central to the Flex forward narrative.

The strategic mandate that emerged through the first years of her tenure centred on portfolio discipline: a deliberate emphasis on higher-margin product and customer categories, measured reduction of exposure to lower-margin consumer electronics assembly, and operational restructuring designed to demonstrate to investors that the EMS model could generate sustained returns above the thin-margin reputation the sector had historically carried. The approach began to show results before the pandemic disrupted the timeline; the subsequent supply chain stress of 2020 through 2022 — which created acute demand for Flex's logistics and sourcing capabilities — accelerated revenue toward the fiscal 2023 peak of approximately $30.0 billion, inclusive of the Nextracker solar tracker business still consolidated within the industrial segment.

| Fiscal Year (ending ~March) | Revenue (USD bn) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FY2020 | $24.2 | Pre-pandemic baseline |
| FY2021 | $24.1 | COVID-19 disruption year |
| FY2022 | $26.0 | Recovery; supply chain demand surge |
| FY2023 | $30.0 | Peak; Nextracker fully consolidated |
| FY2024 | $26.4 | Nextracker partial-year contribution |
| FY2025 | $25.8 | First full year post-separation, two-segment structure |
| FY2026 | $27.9 | CPI carved out as third segment; growth returned |

*Sources: [Flex 2025 Q4 earnings presentation](https://s202.q4cdn.com/732614612/files/doc_earnings/2025/q4/presentation/Flex_EP_FY25Q4.pdf); [Flex FY2026 results](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2026-RESULTS/default.aspx); [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)*

## Nextracker: IPO, Separation, and Strategic Clarity

Within the Flex portfolio, the solar tracker business built inside the industrial segment represented a structural anomaly: a capital-light, high-growth infrastructure technology company whose valuation dynamics were fundamentally different from the assembly-services model governing the rest of the portfolio. Nextracker designed and sold utility-scale solar tracker systems — the mechanical and electronic frameworks that keep photovoltaic panels oriented toward the sun — and had expanded substantially on the back of the global renewable energy buildout.

The decision to separate Nextracker was the most consequential portfolio action of the Advaithi era. In February 2023, Flex completed an initial public offering of Nextracker on the Nasdaq under the ticker NXT. The full separation — the distribution of Flex's remaining ownership interest to Flex shareholders — was completed in January 2024. The transaction crystallised substantial embedded value: Nextracker entered public markets commanding the renewable infrastructure premium its business model warranted, a premium unavailable to Flex shareholders while the solar tracker assets were consolidated inside an EMS holding company.

The separation left Flex with two clearly defined operating segments. Flex Agility Solutions — covering consumer electronics, communications equipment, and lifestyle products — retained the volume-assembly heritage of the Flextronics era. Flex Reliability Solutions — spanning automotive, health solutions, and the industrial category — represented the longer-cycle, higher-complexity customer relationships that the Advaithi strategic emphasis had prioritised. The cleaner two-segment structure gave investors a sharper view of the portfolio mix and gave management a more disciplined internal capital allocation framework.

Advaithi characterised the post-separation Flex as a business with greater strategic clarity, one positioned to pursue the customer categories where Flex's engineering services depth and operational reliability standards commanded a genuine differentiation premium rather than competing solely on assembly cost.

## The AI Data Centre Inflection

The AI data centre infrastructure opportunity that began emerging within Flex Reliability Solutions from 2023 onward was not the product of a deliberate pivot toward the hyperscaler customer category. It was, instead, the consequence of Flex's existing server assembly and rack-level integration capabilities becoming relevant to a new class of demand: the buildout of AI training and inference infrastructure by hyperscale cloud providers and their equipment supply chains.

The industrial category within Flex Reliability Solutions had historically served power and industrial equipment OEMs. As data-center workloads shifted toward AI, Flex disclosed that its existing compute integration, power, and cooling capabilities had begun to pull the company into a different class of infrastructure program. Management did not publicly identify customer names in segment reporting, but it did say the business was increasingly exposed to data-center demand and by fiscal 2026 had become large enough to justify a separate reportable segment. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

The AI data centre opportunity arrived at a structurally significant moment for the post-Nextracker franchise. With the solar tracker business separated, the growth narrative required a forward driver. The hyperscaler AI infrastructure buildout — capital-intensive, scale-demanding, requiring the combination of assembly precision and supply chain coordination that scaled EMS companies are positioned to deliver — offered precisely that, within the segment already representing the higher-margin half of the two-segment structure.

The competitive landscape in AI data centre infrastructure assembly includes Foxconn's server operations, Jabil's diversified manufacturing services, Celestica's data centre infrastructure platform, and Sanmina's high-complexity electronics manufacturing franchise. Differentiation in this category will ultimately turn on engineering services depth, supply chain coordination at the component level — particularly for high-bandwidth memory, networking ASICs, and power delivery components — and the quality and reliability standards hyperscalers impose on infrastructure required to operate continuously at the scale of hundreds of megawatts of compute density.

By the frozen snapshot date, that early-development framing no longer held. Flex had already disclosed that data-center revenue reached about $4.8 billion in fiscal 2025, up roughly 50% year on year, and that in fiscal 2026 it created the CPI segment, which produced $6.614 billion of net sales, up 38% from fiscal 2025, with a 9.2% segment margin. On May 5, 2026, the board said it intended to spin CPI into a separate public company targeted for the first quarter of calendar 2027, with Advaithi set to lead SpinCo and Michael Hartung set to become Flex chief executive. Public filings still did not name the hyperscaler customers individually, but the revenue and reporting changes made clear that the business had moved from emerging adjacency to disclosed strategic center of gravity. [Flex 2025 Q4 earnings presentation](https://s202.q4cdn.com/732614612/files/doc_earnings/2025/q4/presentation/Flex_EP_FY25Q4.pdf), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Flex Announces Intention to Spin Off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure Segment](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Intention-to-Spin-Off-its-Cloud-and-Power-Infrastructure-Segment-into-a-New-Independent-Publicly-Traded-Company/default.aspx)

chapters.title: Flex Agility Solutions, Flex Reliability Solutions, and AI data centre infrastructure assembly
chapters.body:
The legal name change to Flex Ltd took effect in September 2016, but the deeper strategic redesign unfolded more gradually and became visible only after the Nextracker distribution on January 2, 2024. For the twelve months that followed, Flex described itself through Flex Agility Solutions and Flex Reliability Solutions. By the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, management concluded that the data-center opportunity had grown too large to remain buried inside the old structure, created Cloud and Power Infrastructure as a separate reportable segment, and renamed the remaining two segments Integrated Technology Solutions and Regulated Manufacturing Solutions. [Flex constitution, Exhibit 3.01](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637416000007/flex-exx301x93016.htm), [Flex 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637424000021/flex-20240331.htm), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## The Segment Architecture

At March 31, 2026, Flex reported three operating segments:

- **ITS**: communications, high-speed networking, enterprise and satellite communications systems, plus lifestyle categories.
- **RMS**: industrial and mission-critical infrastructure, automotive compute and power electronics, and healthcare manufacturing.
- **CPI**: cloud and cooling systems, advanced liquid cooling, and utility- and facility-level power infrastructure for power-dense compute workloads. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

The fiscal 2026 segment table made the mix shift plain. ITS generated $11.109 billion of net sales and $596 million of segment income; RMS generated $10.191 billion and $611 million; CPI generated $6.614 billion and $610 million. In other words, CPI represented less than a quarter of revenue but had already grown almost as large as the other two segments in segment income. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## ITS: Speed, Variety, and Volume Discipline

ITS was the successor to the faster-cycle side of the old Flex portfolio. It housed communications, enterprise and satellite systems, plus lifestyle categories whose economics depended on rapid product turns, tight supply-chain orchestration, and disciplined working-capital management. In fiscal 2026, ITS revenue slipped 2% year on year, primarily because lifestyle revenue fell 9%, partly offset by a 6% increase in communications. That pattern fit the company's own strategic language: ITS was still a very large business, but it was no longer the principal growth vector. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## RMS: Regulated and Longer-Cycle Programs

RMS carried the businesses Flex most often used to argue that its model had moved beyond commoditized assembly. The 2026 10-K described the segment as industrial and mission-critical automation, automotive compute and power electronics, and healthcare manufacturing for medical devices, drug delivery, and equipment. Revenue in RMS rose 5% in fiscal 2026, driven by 13% growth in Industrial and 5% growth in Healthcare, partly offset by a 2% decline in Automotive. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

Public disclosures supported the qualitative picture. On the automotive side, Flex said it operated 30+ automotive sites, worked with 100+ automotive customers, and supported the sector with compute platforms, power electronics, and motion-and-interface products. It publicly highlighted a March 2025 Catena-X ECU data-exchange launch with BMW Group and an October 2025 Torc collaboration built around an NVIDIA-based platform for autonomous trucks. [Flex Automotive](https://flex.com/industries/automotive), [Flex launches first multiregional Catena-X-based ECU data exchange with BMW Group](https://flex.com/resources/flex-launches-first-multiregional-catena-x-based-ecu-data-exchange-with-bmw-group), [Torc collaborates with Flex on physical AI platform for autonomous trucks](https://flex.com/resources/torc-collaborates-with-flex-on-physical-ai-platform-for-autonomous-trucks)

Healthcare disclosures were similarly concrete where Flex chose to be public. The company opened a new product-introduction center near Boston in March 2025 for healthcare customers in North America, and in November 2025 its Health Solutions business won the PDA Drug Delivery Innovation Award for work with Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany on a connected autoinjector. Those examples did not amount to a complete customer list, but they did support the chapter's broader claim that RMS was anchored in longer-cycle, qualification-heavy programs. [Flex Opens New Product Introduction Center Serving Healthcare Customers in North America](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-Opens-New-Product-Introduction-NPI-Center-Serving-Healthcare-Customers-in-North-America/default.aspx), [Flex and Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, Win 2025 PDA Drug Delivery Innovation Award](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-and-Merck-KGaA-Darmstadt-Germany-Win-2025-PDA-Drug-Delivery-Innovation-Award/default.aspx)

## CPI: The Business That Outgrew the Old Taxonomy

The most important structural fact about Flex by May 2026 was that CPI no longer looked like a subcategory of industrial manufacturing. In the fiscal 2025 fourth-quarter presentation, Flex said data-center revenue had reached approximately $4.8 billion and grown about 50% year on year. One year later the 2026 10-K showed CPI at $6.614 billion of net sales and $610 million of segment income, with 29% growth in Cloud and Cooling and 61% growth in Power. [Flex 2025 Q4 earnings presentation](https://s202.q4cdn.com/732614612/files/doc_earnings/2025/q4/presentation/Flex_EP_FY25Q4.pdf), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

The operating footprint around that segment had also become more visible. Flex launched an AI infrastructure platform in October 2025 that it said could cut deployment times by up to 30%. Its modular rack-level CDU scaled from 600 kilowatts to 1.8 megawatts. In November 2025 it deployed a rack-level liquid-cooling demonstration at Equinix's co-innovation facility in Ashburn. In March 2026 it said it was already building prefabricated modular solutions for hyperscalers, including at a 400,000-square-foot Dallas facility purpose-built for data-center infrastructure. [Flex announces new AI infrastructure platform to speed deployment by up to 30%](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-announces-new-AI-infrastructure-platform-to-speed-deployment-by-up-to-30/default.aspx), [Flex Expands Data Center Cooling Portfolio with Launch of Modular Rack-Level Coolant Distribution Unit](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-Expands-Data-Center-Cooling-Portfolio-with-Launch-of-Modular-Rack-Level-Coolant-Distribution-Unit/default.aspx), [Flex Expands Liquid Cooling Footprint at Equinix Co-Innovation Facility](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-Expands-Liquid-Cooling-Footprint-at-Equinix-Co-Innovation-Facility/default.aspx), [Flex Accelerates AI Factory Deployment with NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Reference Designs](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Accelerates-AI-Factory-Deployment-with-NVIDIA-Omniverse-DSX-Reference-Designs/default.aspx)

## What the Structure Meant

The old two-segment story had implied a cleaner split between fast-cycle and long-cycle manufacturing. The 2026 disclosures showed something more consequential: Flex had effectively incubated a systems-integration and power-and-cooling business large enough to become a third segment and then large enough to be spun out. That did not invalidate the original ITS-versus-RMS framing. It did, however, explain why the frozen-window dossier could no longer talk about Flex as though the data-center build-out were just another industrial adjacency. The financial statements had already elevated it beyond that.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, margin expansion, Nextracker separation framework
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Arc Under Advaithi

The revenue curve across Revathi Advaithi's tenure was no longer adequately described by the old pre-spin narrative of a fiscal 2023 peak followed by a post-Nextracker reset. By the frozen snapshot date the more relevant sequence was: $30.0 billion in fiscal 2023 with Nextracker still consolidated; $26.4 billion in fiscal 2024 as the deconsolidation took hold; $25.8 billion in fiscal 2025 as the first full post-Nextracker baseline; and then $27.914 billion in fiscal 2026 as data-center and power demand re-accelerated the business. [Flex 2025 Q4 earnings presentation](https://s202.q4cdn.com/732614612/files/doc_earnings/2025/q4/presentation/Flex_EP_FY25Q4.pdf), [Flex FY2026 results](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2026-RESULTS/default.aspx), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Key Context |
|---|---|---|
| FY2020 | $24.2 | Advaithi's first full year as CEO |
| FY2021 | $24.1 | Pandemic disruption, early restructuring |
| FY2022 | $26.0 | Recovery and supply-chain surge |
| FY2023 | $30.0 | Nextracker still fully consolidated |
| FY2024 | $26.4 | Nextracker distribution completed January 2, 2024 |
| FY2025 | $25.8 | First full year without Nextracker |
| FY2026 | $27.9 | CPI created as third segment; growth returned |

The point was not simply that revenue recovered in fiscal 2026. It was that the source of growth changed. The March 2026 year saw ITS revenue decline 2%, RMS rise 5%, and CPI rise 38%. The recovering top line therefore came from a business that had previously been submerged inside the old FAS/FRS split. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## Nextracker Separation: Mechanics and Consequences

Nextracker's path to separation had two distinct dates, not one. The registration statement for Nextracker's IPO was declared effective on February 8, 2023, the shares began trading on February 9, and the offering closed on February 13. Flex still consolidated the business after that flotation because it retained control. Full separation came only on January 2, 2024, when Flex distributed its remaining interest pro rata to Flex shareholders of record as of December 29, 2023. Flex's fiscal 2024 filings said shareholders received roughly 0.17 shares of Nextracker Class A common stock for each Flex ordinary share held, with cash in lieu of fractional shares. [Nextracker 2023 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1852131/000185213123000007/nxt-20230929.htm), [Flex 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637424000021/flex-20240331.htm)

That structure mattered because it explained why the revenue step-down from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 did not constitute like-for-like deterioration. The 2026 10-K explicitly presented Nextracker's historical results as discontinued operations, making the post-spin business easier to read. What investors were left with was not a diminished solar-plus-EMS conglomerate, but a narrower company whose quality of earnings would be tested on its own terms. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## Margin Expansion: From Thesis to Measured Outcome

The simplest proof that Advaithi's operating thesis had worked lay in margins. In the fiscal 2025 fourth-quarter presentation, Flex showed adjusted operating margin rising from 4.8% in fiscal 2024 to 5.7% in fiscal 2025. In the fiscal 2026 results release, that figure rose again to 6.3%, another company record. Adjusted operating income climbed from $1.459 billion in fiscal 2025 to $1.764 billion in fiscal 2026, while adjusted EPS rose from $2.65 to $3.30. [Flex 2025 Q4 earnings presentation](https://s202.q4cdn.com/732614612/files/doc_earnings/2025/q4/presentation/Flex_EP_FY25Q4.pdf), [Flex FY2026 results](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2026-RESULTS/default.aspx)

At the segment level, the quality differential was even clearer. Fiscal 2026 segment margins were 5.4% for ITS, 6.0% for RMS, and 9.2% for CPI. The new infrastructure segment was therefore not just the fastest grower but also the most profitable reportable business inside the company at the moment management chose to separate it. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## Cash Flow, Repurchases, and Capital Allocation

Free cash flow remained above the billion-dollar line in both fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026, though it eased modestly from $1.082 billion to $1.060 billion. That still gave management room to keep buying back stock while pursuing acquisitions. The 2026 10-K said Flex repurchased 19.2 million shares for $944 million during fiscal 2026 and still had $1.1 billion remaining under the current authorization at March 31, 2026. [Flex FY2026 results](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2026-RESULTS/default.aspx), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

The acquisition record was no longer incidental. JetCool widened Flex's direct-liquid-cooling capability in November 2024. Crown, acquired for $325 million in December 2024, added integrated power-distribution and protection systems. Electrical Power Products, acquired in May 2026, deepened U.S. critical-power exposure. In the 2026 filing, management directly tied these acquisitions to the EMS + Products + Services strategy and to data-center customer needs around power, heat, and scale. [Flex Acquires JetCool](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2024/Flex-Acquires-JetCool-to-Expand-Data-Center-and-Power-Portfolio/default.aspx), [Flex Completes Acquisition of Crown Technical Systems](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2024/Flex-Completes-Acquisition-of-Crown-Technical-Systems/default.aspx), [Flex Announces Agreement to Acquire Electrical Power Products](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Agreement-to-Acquire-Electrical-Power-Products-EP/default.aspx), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## The New Financial Baseline

By May 2026, the most useful baseline for valuation work was no longer fiscal 2025 alone. It was a three-part picture:

1. A continuing advanced-manufacturing platform of ITS and RMS that together generated roughly $21.3 billion of fiscal 2026 revenue.
2. A CPI operation with $6.614 billion of revenue, 9.2% segment margin, and 38% growth.
3. A board-approved separation plan that would split those pieces into two companies, with SpinCo targeted for 65% to 75% revenue growth in fiscal 2027 and 80%+ in fiscal 2028. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Flex Announces Intention to Spin Off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure Segment](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Intention-to-Spin-Off-its-Cloud-and-Power-Infrastructure-Segment-into-a-New-Independent-Publicly-Traded-Company/default.aspx)

That was a different analytical object from the one the market had been asked to value in fiscal 2024. The financial deep dive therefore had to treat the Nextracker separation not as the end of the story but as the first rehearsal for a second, more consequential unbundling.

chapters.title: Post-Advaithi quarters through Nextracker separation and AI inflection
chapters.body:
## The Advaithi Earnings Record, Quarter by Quarter

By the frozen snapshot date, the old quarter-by-quarter earnings story had collapsed into two linked arcs: first, the removal of Nextracker from the numbers; second, the emergence of CPI as a separately reported growth and margin engine. Flex's fiscal 2026 results were the first full-year disclosure in which that second arc was impossible to miss. [Flex FY2026 results](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2026-RESULTS/default.aspx), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

| Fiscal Year (March end) | Revenue (USD billions) | Key Event |
|---|---|---|
| FY2020 | $24.2 | Advaithi's first full year |
| FY2021 | $24.1 | Pandemic disruption; restructuring continues |
| FY2022 | $26.0 | Recovery and supply-chain demand |
| FY2023 | $30.0 | Nextracker still fully consolidated |
| FY2024 | $26.4 | Nextracker distribution completed January 2, 2024 |
| FY2025 | $25.8 | First full post-separation baseline |
| FY2026 | $27.9 | CPI established as third segment; spin announced |

The February 2023 Nextracker flotation was only the opening move. The IPO registration became effective on February 8, 2023, the shares began trading on February 9, and the offer closed on February 13; Flex kept consolidating Nextracker until the January 2, 2024 distribution of its remaining interest. That is why fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025 should be read as transition years rather than clean operating comparisons. [Nextracker 2023 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1852131/000185213123000007/nxt-20230929.htm), [Flex 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637424000021/flex-20240331.htm)

## Fiscal 2025: The Last Year of the Old Reporting Frame

Fiscal 2025 mattered because it was the first full year in which the post-Nextracker business stood on its own. Flex reported $25.8 billion of revenue, adjusted operating income of $1.459 billion, adjusted EPS of $2.65, and adjusted operating margin of 5.7%. In the accompanying presentation, management said data-center revenue had reached about $4.8 billion and had grown roughly 50% year on year, putting hard numbers behind what had previously been a mostly qualitative growth narrative. [Flex 2025 Q4 earnings presentation](https://s202.q4cdn.com/732614612/files/doc_earnings/2025/q4/presentation/Flex_EP_FY25Q4.pdf), [Flex FY2025 results](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2025-RESULTS/default.aspx)

That same fiscal 2025 record also marked the beginning of an executive handover inside the finance function. Paul Lundstrom, who had joined Flex as CFO on September 1, 2020 from Aerojet Rocketdyne after senior finance roles at United Technologies, stepped down effective July 31, 2024. Jaime Martinez served as interim CFO from August 1, 2024 until Kevin Krumm joined on January 6, 2025. [Flex Announces Chief Financial Officer Transition](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2020/Flex-Announces-Chief-Financial-Officer-Transition/default.aspx), [FLEX REPORTS FIRST QUARTER FISCAL 2025 RESULTS, ANNOUNCES CFO TRANSITION](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2024/FLEX-REPORTS-FIRST-QUARTER-FISCAL-2025-RESULTS-ANNOUNCES-CHIEF-FINANCIAL-OFFICER-TRANSITION/default.aspx), [Flex Announces Kevin Krumm as Chief Financial Officer](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2024/Flex-Announces-Kevin-Krumm-as-Chief-Financial-Officer/default.aspx), [Flex 2025 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000130817925000552/flex014214-def14a.htm)

## Fiscal 2026: CPI Moved to the Center

The fiscal 2026 earnings release changed the story from stabilization to acceleration. Flex reported $27.9 billion of revenue, up 8% year on year; adjusted operating income of $1.764 billion; adjusted EPS of $3.30; and free cash flow of $1.060 billion. The March 2026 quarter itself came in at $7.5 billion of revenue and 6.7% adjusted operating margin, the sixth consecutive quarter at 6% or higher. [Flex FY2026 results](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2026-RESULTS/default.aspx)

The filing showed where that acceleration had come from. ITS net sales fell by $0.2 billion. RMS rose by $0.5 billion. CPI rose by $1.8 billion to $6.614 billion, driven by 29% growth in Cloud and Cooling and 61% growth in Power. CPI segment income reached $610 million, nearly matching RMS at $611 million and edging past ITS at $596 million. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## What Management Actually Reported

The important point was that management stopped asking investors to infer the scale of the AI-linked build-out from scattered comments on calls. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 it changed the segment reporting itself. FAS became ITS; FRS became RMS; Cloud and Power Infrastructure became a standalone reporting segment. The filing described CPI as focused on integrated compute systems, power, and cooling technologies for large-scale cloud, data-center, and AI-enabled infrastructure deployments. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

The public customer detail stayed limited. Flex still did not name hyperscaler customers in the 10-K, and no single customer exceeded 10% of fiscal 2026 net sales. But the risk-factor language made the dependence visible in another way: the company said customer concentration was particularly pronounced in CPI, where a limited number of hyperscale cloud providers, colocation companies, and large enterprise data-center operators represented a substantial portion of demand. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## The May 2026 Break in the Narrative

On May 5, 2026, the board turned that earnings profile into a structural transaction. Flex said it intended to spin off CPI as a tax-free transaction for U.S. shareholders, targeted for the first quarter of calendar 2027. Revathi Advaithi would become chief executive of SpinCo and serve as Flex chairman for a transitional period; Michael Hartung would become chief executive of Flex. SpinCo was targeted for 65% to 75% revenue growth in fiscal 2027 and 80%+ in fiscal 2028. [Flex Announces Intention to Spin Off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure Segment](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Intention-to-Spin-Off-its-Cloud-and-Power-Infrastructure-Segment-into-a-New-Independent-Publicly-Traded-Company/default.aspx)

The earnings story therefore no longer ended with a question about whether AI demand would offset the Nextracker exit. By the end of the frozen window, AI-linked infrastructure had already done so. The question had become whether Flex was now spinning out the very segment that had driven the company's most visible improvement in growth and mix.

chapters.title: Advaithi, Lundstrom CFO, segment leadership, Adamovich-Lead-Independent board
chapters.body:
## The CEO Succession: Advaithi's February 2019 Mandate

When Revathi Advaithi succeeded Mike McNamara as President and Chief Executive Officer on 11 February 2019, she brought operating credentials from the Eaton Corporation electrical franchise — twenty-four years across Eaton and Honeywell in power management, supply chain, and industrial manufacturing. Per the [Flex 2025 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000130817925000552/flex014214-def14a.htm): Eaton from 1995, a Shanghai assignment running the Electrical Sector, a six-year Honeywell detour (2002–2008), then return to Eaton rising to President and COO, Electrical Sector globally (September 2015 until her departure). Education: mechanical engineering from BITS Pilani, MBA from Thunderbird.

The 2019 mandate: reverse margin compression, shed lower-return product lines, and position for higher-value EMS categories in automotive, medical devices, and AI data centre infrastructure. Advaithi labelled the programme "Flex Forward." The Nextracker separation was the most visible act — leaving Flex as a pure-play EMS company.

In the June 2025 proxy, Advaithi said fiscal 2025 had marked an inflection point and framed the next phase of the strategy around extending Flex beyond core manufacturing and supply-chain services into a broader mix of products and value-added services. The financial delivery behind that declaration was measurable. [Flex 2025 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000130817925000552/flex014214-def14a.htm) Fiscal year 2025, ended March 31, 2025, produced record adjusted operating margin of 5.7% and adjusted EPS of $2.65; the accompanying earnings presentation said data-center revenue reached about $4.8 billion, up roughly 50% year on year. By fiscal 2026, Flex reported record adjusted operating margin of 6.3%, adjusted EPS of $3.30, and free cash flow of $1.060 billion. The company also disclosed that CPI had become a $6.614 billion revenue segment with a 9.2% segment margin before the announced spin. [Flex 2025 Q4 earnings presentation](https://s202.q4cdn.com/732614612/files/doc_earnings/2025/q4/presentation/Flex_EP_FY25Q4.pdf), [Flex FY2026 results](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2026-RESULTS/default.aspx), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## CFO Architecture: Lundstrom, the Transition, and Krumm

The financial officer cadence that accompanied Advaithi's first six years at the helm involved three distinct chapters. Christopher Collier, who had been CFO under McNamara, remained through the early Advaithi period. Paul R. Lundstrom joined as Chief Financial Officer effective September 1, 2020. Flex's announcement said he had most recently served as vice president of finance and chief financial officer of Aerojet Rocketdyne Holdings and had previously held several division-CFO and corporate finance roles during 19 years at United Technologies. [Flex Announces Chief Financial Officer Transition](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2020/Flex-Announces-Chief-Financial-Officer-Transition/default.aspx) Lundstrom's tenure straddled the entire Nextracker arc: the IPO structuring, the partial separation financing, and the January 2024 full spin-off. He also presided over the sustained buyback programme and the rating-agency engagement that accompanied the return of capital to shareholders. 8-K filings signed by Lundstrom as CFO appear in SEC records from October 2020 through mid-2024.

On 31 July 2024, Lundstrom resigned. The 2025 proxy statement confirmed that he departed before fiscal year 2025 concluded and accordingly received no annual bonus payout for that year. The company appointed Jaime Martinez, a senior internal finance executive, as Interim Chief Financial Officer from 1 August 2024 while a successor search ran in parallel. Martinez served for five months before reverting to his prior role as Senior Vice President, Finance on 5 January 2025.

Kevin Krumm was named Chief Financial Officer effective 6 January 2025. The biographical record in the 2025 proxy places him, age 51, as a career finance executive with deep manufacturing and services company experience: a fifteen-year tenure at Ecolab, the water and hygiene solutions company, where he led regional finance teams across Europe, the Middle East and Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and directed international integration work on a major acquisition, culminating as Corporate Treasurer and Senior Vice President of Global Finance Shared Services from December 2019. From September 2021 to late 2024 Krumm served as Executive Vice President and CFO of APi Group Corporation, a global life safety and fire protection services business. His educational background — a bachelor's in accounting from the University of Northern Iowa, an MBA from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, and early career roles at PwC, Arthur Andersen and Deloitte with heavy M&A and corporate finance emphasis — brings a different profile to Flex than Lundstrom's defence-sector CFO background. Krumm's Ecolab years in particular suggest familiarity with complex multinational manufacturing operations across Asia and Europe, directly applicable to Flex's global footprint of over 48 million square feet across approximately 30 countries.

## Segment Leadership and the Hartung Consolidation

On 26 July 2024, Michael P. Hartung was promoted to President and Chief Commercial Officer, assuming oversight of both FAS and FRS — consolidating segment P&L leadership that had been split between Doug Britt (Agility) and Francois Barbier (Reliability). Hartung joined Flex in 2007 from Solectron and served as President of Agility Solutions from April 2020.

Simultaneously, Kwanghooi (Hooi) Tan, a more than 20-year Flex veteran, became COO on October 1, 2024 after serving as president of global operations and components. By the frozen snapshot date, Flex's public leadership page showed Kevin Krumm as CFO, Hooi Tan as COO, Michael Hartung as president and chief commercial officer, Riccardo Butta as president of Health Solutions, Rob Campbell as president of Communications, Enterprise and Cloud, Christopher Butler as president of Embedded and Critical Power, Dennis Kirkpatrick as president of Lifestyle, Consumer Devices, and Core Industrial, Mike Thoeny as president of Automotive, and Scott Offer as executive vice president and general counsel. [Flex 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000130817925000555/flex014214-ars.pdf), [Flex leadership](https://flex.com/company/our-leadership)

## Board Governance: From Capellas to the Watkins Independent Chair

The Flex board undertook its most visible governance transition on 8 August 2024, the date of the company's 2024 Annual General Meeting in Austin. Michael D. Capellas, who had served as Chairman and had provided continuity through the Nextracker separation, retired and did not stand for re-election. William D. Watkins, a director since 2009 and the longest-tenured independent director on the current board, succeeded to the Independent Chair role. The 2025 proxy confirmed the designation: Watkins was styled as "Independent Chair of the Board" with a formal charter delineating his oversight responsibilities — CEO succession, Board evaluation, executive sessions, and liaison duties between non-employee directors and management.

Watkins carried the record of a career-long technology manufacturing executive: COO and then CEO of Seagate Technology from 2000 to 2009, responsible for Seagate's hard disk drive operations and R&D; subsequent CEO tenures at Bridgelux (LED technology) and Imergy Power Systems (energy storage). He concurrently sits on the board of Nextracker Inc., the company spun off from Flex in 2023, providing an unusual governance thread connecting the former parent with the most strategically significant divestiture of the Advaithi era.

The nine-director board presented in the 2025 proxy reflected a substantial refreshment cycle that began in 2020. Charles K. Stevens III, the former Executive Vice President and CFO of General Motors, chairs the Audit Committee and brings automotive manufacturing financial expertise directly relevant to the Flex Reliability Solutions automotive sub-segment; his 40-year GM career included regional CFO roles across North America, South America, Asia-Pacific, and Europe. Erin L. McSweeney, Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer of UnitedHealth Group, chairs the Compensation and People Committee. John D. Harris II, who served until retirement as Vice President of Business Development at Raytheon Company and Chief Executive Officer of Raytheon International, and Patrick J. Ward, the former Vice President and CFO of Cummins Inc., both serve on the Audit Committee as designated financial experts. Ward, a Cummins lifer from 1987 through 2019, brings industrial manufacturing CFO experience that parallels Stevens's automotive credentials in the Reliability Solutions context.

Maryrose Sylvester, the former President and CEO of Current (GE's digital power business) and US Managing Director of ABB's electrification division, brings energy infrastructure and global supply chain experience. Michael E. Hurlston, who became President and CEO of Lumentum Holdings in February 2025 — a Flex customer — was reclassified as non-independent under Nasdaq rules at that point and concluded his Audit Committee service; he remains on the board without committee assignment, contributing semiconductor industry expertise from prior executive roles at Broadcom, Finisar, and Synaptics. Lay Koon Tan, the sole Singapore-resident director and a board member since 2012, brings semiconductor packaging CEO experience from his foundational role building STATS ChipPAC Ltd., and provides the Singapore-incorporated Flex's mandatory local-resident director requirement under the Companies Act 1967.

The aggregate committee structure allocates financial oversight (Stevens as Audit Chair, Harris and Ward as members, Lay Koon Tan as member) to a group with three designated audit committee financial experts. Compensation governance sits with McSweeney, Sylvester, and Ward. Watkins chairs the Nominating, Governance and Public Responsibility Committee alongside McSweeney and Stevens, giving the governance committee significant overlap with the Audit Committee in risk oversight.

The board, in its proxy-disclosed self-assessment, emphasised the pace of refreshment: five new independent directors since June 2020 (Harris, Hurlston, McSweeney, Sylvester, Ward), an average nominee tenure of 7.0 years, and a gender representation of 33% women and 33% directors from underrepresented racial or ethnic groups. The governance structure as of the frozen snapshot date — Advaithi as sole management director, Watkins as independent chair, and three fully independent committees — was also already a transition structure. On May 5, 2026, Flex said Advaithi would become chief executive of SpinCo and serve as chairman of Flex for a transitional period following the spin, while Michael Hartung would be named chief executive of Flex. [Flex 2025 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000130817925000552/flex014214-def14a.htm), [Flex Announces Intention to Spin Off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure Segment](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Intention-to-Spin-Off-its-Cloud-and-Power-Infrastructure-Segment-into-a-New-Independent-Publicly-Traded-Company/default.aspx)

---

*Sources: [Flex Ltd. DEF 14A, filed 24 June 2025, accession 0001308179-25-000552](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000130817925000552/flex014214-def14a.htm); [Flex Ltd. 8-K dated 8 August 2024, accession 0000866374-24-000036](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637424000036/flex-20240808.htm); [Flex Ltd. submission data, SEC EDGAR CIK 0000866374](https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0000866374.json).*

Earlier draft references to John D. Adamovich Jr. as a Flex lead independent director were not supported by SEC-filed proxy statements covering fiscal 2020 through fiscal 2025. Those filings instead showed Michael D. Capellas as chairman until the August 2024 annual meeting and William D. Watkins as independent chair thereafter. [Flex 2025 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000130817925000552/flex014214-def14a.htm), [Flex 8-K, August 8 2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637424000036/flex-20240808.htm)

chapters.title: Multi-segment customers, hyperscaler AI emerging, and the global manufacturing footprint
chapters.body:
## Customer Breadth Across the Reporting Structure

Flex's filings did not publish a clean named-customer roster by segment, and the company did not identify any single customer accounting for more than 10% of fiscal 2026 net sales. But the 2026 10-K did disclose that the ten largest customers still represented 45% of revenue, which meant concentration remained meaningful even without a dominant account. The more reliable way to describe customer breadth inside the frozen window was therefore through public examples, end-market disclosures, and geography rather than through speculative master lists. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## Automotive and Regulated Programs

In automotive, Flex publicly said it operated 30+ automotive sites, served 100+ automotive customers, and supported the market with compute platforms, power electronics, and motion-and-interface products. The public record offered several concrete examples. In March 2025, Flex said it had launched a multiregional Catena-X ECU data-exchange use case with BMW Group. In April 2025, it said its Jupiter Compute Platform and Backup DC/DC Converter had won two Automotive News PACE Awards, and that both platforms were already being adopted by global automakers. In October 2025, Flex published a case study on Torc's autonomous-truck program built around an NVIDIA-based Flex hardware platform. [Flex Automotive](https://flex.com/industries/automotive), [Flex launches first multiregional Catena-X-based ECU data exchange with BMW Group](https://flex.com/resources/flex-launches-first-multiregional-catena-x-based-ecu-data-exchange-with-bmw-group), [Flex Wins Two 2025 PACE Awards for Innovation in Automotive Compute and Power Electronics](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-Wins-Two-2025-PACE-Awards-for-Innovation-in-Automotive-Compute-and-Power-Electronics/), [Torc collaborates with Flex on physical AI platform for autonomous trucks](https://flex.com/resources/torc-collaborates-with-flex-on-physical-ai-platform-for-autonomous-trucks)

Healthcare disclosures were similarly selective but tangible. The 2026 10-K described RMS healthcare as regulated manufacturing for medical devices, drug delivery, and equipment. In March 2025, Flex opened a new product-introduction center near Boston to serve healthcare customers in North America. In November 2025, its Health Solutions business won the PDA Drug Delivery Innovation Award with Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany for a connected autoinjector, and said the companies had collaborated for nearly two decades. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Flex Opens New Product Introduction Center Serving Healthcare Customers in North America](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-Opens-New-Product-Introduction-NPI-Center-Serving-Healthcare-Customers-in-North-America/default.aspx), [Flex and Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, Win 2025 PDA Drug Delivery Innovation Award](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-and-Merck-KGaA-Darmstadt-Germany-Win-2025-PDA-Drug-Delivery-Innovation-Award/default.aspx)

## Data-Center and Infrastructure Customers

Where the dossier's earlier draft had overreached was in naming specific hyperscalers without primary-source support. Flex's filings did not do that. What they did say was that customer concentration was particularly pronounced in CPI and that a limited number of hyperscale cloud providers, colocation companies, and large enterprise data-center operators represented a substantial portion of demand. Public examples around the edges of that business were nevertheless plentiful. Flex deployed a rack-level liquid-cooling demonstration at Equinix's co-innovation facility in Ashburn in November 2025, and in March 2026 said it was building prefabricated modular solutions for hyperscalers at its 400,000-square-foot Dallas facility. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Flex Expands Liquid Cooling Footprint at Equinix Co-Innovation Facility](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-Expands-Liquid-Cooling-Footprint-at-Equinix-Co-Innovation-Facility/default.aspx), [Flex Accelerates AI Factory Deployment with NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Reference Designs](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Accelerates-AI-Factory-Deployment-with-NVIDIA-Omniverse-DSX-Reference-Designs/default.aspx)

Those disclosures were enough to support a more careful claim: that Flex had real public proof points in AI infrastructure, but had not, as of the frozen date, chosen to name the largest cloud accounts in SEC filings.

## The Geographic Footprint Behind the Customer Mix

The supply chain disclosures were more specific than the customer disclosures. Flex said it operated across approximately 30 countries. In fiscal 2026, the Americas accounted for $13.820 billion of revenue, or 50% of net sales; Asia accounted for $8.401 billion, or 30%; and Europe accounted for $5.693 billion, or 20%. By country of manufacture, Mexico accounted for 25% of revenue, the U.S. 19%, China 16%, and Malaysia 11%. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

That footprint was not just inherited scale. It was a commercial asset. The automotive page emphasized regionalized execution across 30+ automotive sites. The 2026 NVIDIA reference-design announcement highlighted 18+ million square feet across 35+ locations in the Americas. The 2024 and 2026 filings both framed the global network as a response to customer demands for resiliency, faster time to market, and compliance with shifting sourcing rules. [Flex Automotive](https://flex.com/industries/automotive), [Flex Accelerates AI Factory Deployment with NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Reference Designs](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Accelerates-AI-Factory-Deployment-with-NVIDIA-Omniverse-DSX-Reference-Designs/default.aspx), [Flex 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637424000021/flex-20240331.htm), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## What Could Be Said Reliably

The fact-checked version of the customer chapter therefore looked more restrained but also more defensible. Flex was not a company that disclosed customer logos in every vertical. It was, however, a company that publicly demonstrated BMW, Torc, Merck KGaA, and Equinix relationships; disclosed broad concentration metrics; and published a geographic revenue map detailed enough to show where customer demand was actually being manufactured. That was a better evidentiary base than the unsupported omnibus rosters in the earlier draft.

chapters.title: Where Flex sits against Foxconn, Jabil, Celestica, Sanmina, broader EMS competitive set
chapters.body:
## The EMS League Table, Redrawn

The competitive picture at the frozen snapshot date was easier to describe than to simplify. Flex no longer sat above every U.S.-listed EMS peer by revenue: Jabil reported $29.8 billion for fiscal 2025, versus Flex's $27.914 billion for fiscal 2026. But Flex still remained in the top U.S.-listed tier, materially larger than Celestica and Sanmina and structurally more diversified than the companies whose equity stories had become more explicitly tied to AI infrastructure. [Jabil FY2025 results](https://investors.jabil.com/news/news-details/2025/Jabil-Posts-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Celestica FY2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1030894/000103089426000006/cls-20251231prcondensedfs.htm), [Sanmina FY2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/897723/000089772325000036/sanmina_exx991xsep272025.htm)

| Peer | Ticker | Latest disclosed annual revenue within frozen window | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Jabil | JBL | $29.8B | Larger U.S.-listed peer; AI, healthcare, industrial mix |
| **Flex** | **FLEX** | **$27.9B** | Three-segment structure by March 2026; CPI spin announced |
| Celestica | CLS | $12.39B | AI and cloud concentration drew a valuation premium |
| Sanmina | SANM | $8.1B | High-complexity IMS model, including cloud and AI infrastructure |

Foxconn remained in a separate scale category altogether. Hon Hai's own site described its FY2025 and 4Q25 results as a March 16, 2026 corporate event, reinforcing the basic competitive truth that Foxconn was much larger than the rest of the peer set and not best understood as a like-for-like valuation comparable to Flex. [Hon Hai press center](https://www.honhai.com/en-us/press-center/press-releases/latest-news/1947)

## Jabil: The Closest Scale Comparator

Jabil was the cleanest revenue comparator because it lived in the same broad U.S.-listed manufacturing universe while also having executed its own portfolio simplification. In September 2023, Jabil announced a definitive agreement to divest its Mobility business to BYD Electronic for $2.2 billion; it completed the transaction on December 29, 2023. By fiscal 2025, Jabil reported $29.8 billion of net revenue and highlighted AI-driven demand across capital equipment, data centers, and networking as a key driver. [Jabil Announces Definitive Agreement to Divest Mobility Business for $2.2 Billion](https://investors.jabil.com/news/news-details/2023/Jabil-Announces-Definitive-Agreement-to-Divest-Mobility-Business-for-2.2-Billion/default.aspx), [Jabil Completes the Divestiture of Mobility Business](https://investors.jabil.com/news/news-details/2023/Jabil-Completes-the-Divestiture-of-Mobility-Business/default.aspx), [Jabil FY2025 results](https://investors.jabil.com/news/news-details/2025/Jabil-Posts-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/)

That put Flex and Jabil in a more symmetrical relationship than the earlier draft suggested. Flex still had the stronger explicit automotive-manufacturing identity in its public materials, while Jabil was more willing to foreground AI data-center demand in investor communications. But it was no longer defensible to claim that Flex was categorically larger.

## Celestica: The Concentration Premium

Celestica's filings showed why public markets had treated it differently. For 2025, Celestica reported $12.39 billion of revenue, GAAP operating margin of 8.4%, and adjusted operating margin of 7.5%, with customer demand particularly strong in its cloud and connectivity systems business. That was far smaller revenue than Flex, but the mix was more concentrated around the exact AI-and-cloud categories the market most wanted exposure to. [Celestica FY2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1030894/000103089426000006/cls-20251231prcondensedfs.htm)

For Flex, Celestica was the live counterfactual. Celestica showed what happened when the market rewarded concentrated AI exposure. Flex showed what happened when the same broad end-market opportunity was still embedded inside a more diversified industrial and manufacturing platform.

## Sanmina: Complexity and Selectivity

Sanmina's fiscal 2025 results reinforced its position as a smaller but still relevant high-complexity competitor. The company reported $8.1 billion of revenue, 4.4% GAAP operating margin, and 5.7% non-GAAP operating margin, while also citing strength in communications networks and cloud and AI infrastructure. It was not a scale peer to Flex, but it remained a real competitor in the higher-reliability slices of the market where qualification, traceability, and manufacturing discipline mattered more than pure volume. [Sanmina FY2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/897723/000089772325000036/sanmina_exx991xsep272025.htm)

## Flex's Differentiation

The fact-checked competitive case for Flex rested on three supported points rather than a long list of generalized boasts.

First, the company still combined unusual scale with diversification. The 2026 10-K showed $27.914 billion of annual revenue spread across ITS, RMS, and CPI, with no single customer above 10% of sales. That made Flex less concentrated than pure AI plays and less exposed than companies built around a single large end-market. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

Second, Flex had unusually strong public proof points in automotive and regulated manufacturing. The company said it served 100+ automotive customers across 30+ automotive sites, had launched a Catena-X ECU data exchange with BMW Group, and had won two 2025 PACE Awards for its automotive compute and power-electronics platforms. That was a materially different commercial story from peers that were mainly pitching infrastructure exposure. [Flex Automotive](https://flex.com/industries/automotive), [Flex launches first multiregional Catena-X-based ECU data exchange with BMW Group](https://flex.com/resources/flex-launches-first-multiregional-catena-x-based-ecu-data-exchange-with-bmw-group), [Flex Wins Two 2025 PACE Awards](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-Wins-Two-2025-PACE-Awards-for-Innovation-in-Automotive-Compute-and-Power-Electronics/)

Third, the company had, by May 2026, already isolated the business that looked most like the market's preferred AI-infrastructure asset. CPI reached $6.614 billion of net sales and $610 million of segment income in fiscal 2026, and the board announced plans to spin it out. That meant the market was no longer being asked to infer hidden value from an unsegmented infrastructure business; it was being asked to decide what each half of the company should look like on its own. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Flex Announces Intention to Spin Off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure Segment](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Intention-to-Spin-Off-its-Cloud-and-Power-Infrastructure-Segment-into-a-New-Independent-Publicly-Traded-Company/default.aspx)

## The New Competitive Front

That left Flex in a more precise competitive position than the earlier draft captured. It was not the biggest U.S.-listed EMS peer by revenue, but it was still one of the two largest. It was not as concentrated an AI story as Celestica, but it had already built and segmented a large infrastructure business. And it was not as narrowly specialized as Sanmina, but it had deeper regulated-manufacturing and automotive proof points than the AI-pure-play narrative alone would suggest. The competitive question heading into the second half of the 2020s was therefore not whether Flex belonged in the top tier. It was whether the separation of CPI would finally let the market value the top tier in two distinct pieces instead of one blended multiple.

chapters.title: From 1969 founding through rebrand, Advaithi, Nextracker, AI inflection
chapters.body:
*Corporate history, including the 2007 Solectron deal and the 2016 legal name change from Flextronics International Ltd. to Flex Ltd., is detailed in the Corporate History chapter.*

*The Nextracker IPO and January 2, 2024 full distribution are detailed in the Financial Deep Dive chapter.*

## The AI Data Centre Inflection

The research gap in the earlier draft was not whether Flex had disclosed enough to prove an AI-linked business existed; by the frozen window it plainly had. The company said data-center revenue reached approximately $4.8 billion in fiscal 2025, up roughly 50% year on year. In fiscal 2026 it created CPI as a separate reportable segment, reported $6.614 billion of net sales and $610 million of segment income there, and then on May 5, 2026 announced plans to spin the business into a separate public company targeted for the first quarter of calendar 2027. [Flex 2025 Q4 earnings presentation](https://s202.q4cdn.com/732614612/files/doc_earnings/2025/q4/presentation/Flex_EP_FY25Q4.pdf), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Flex Announces Intention to Spin Off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure Segment](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Intention-to-Spin-Off-its-Cloud-and-Power-Infrastructure-Segment-into-a-New-Independent-Publicly-Traded-Company/default.aspx)

The operational record around that inflection was equally tangible. Flex launched an AI infrastructure platform in October 2025 that it said could speed deployment by up to 30%, deployed liquid-cooling infrastructure at Equinix's co-innovation facility in November 2025, and in March 2026 said it was building prefabricated modular solutions for hyperscalers at a 400,000-square-foot Dallas facility. The catalyst set had therefore shifted from conjecture to disclosed operating scale and a board-approved separation plan. [Flex announces new AI infrastructure platform to speed deployment by up to 30%](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-announces-new-AI-infrastructure-platform-to-speed-deployment-by-up-to-30/default.aspx), [Flex Expands Liquid Cooling Footprint at Equinix Co-Innovation Facility](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-Expands-Liquid-Cooling-Footprint-at-Equinix-Co-Innovation-Facility/default.aspx), [Flex Accelerates AI Factory Deployment with NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Reference Designs](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Accelerates-AI-Factory-Deployment-with-NVIDIA-Omniverse-DSX-Reference-Designs/default.aspx)

chapters.title: EMS operational know-how, complex-systems assembly capability, R&D framework
chapters.body:
## Manufacturing DNA: The Operational Core

Flex's most defensible intellectual property claim remained process breadth rather than a single branded invention. The fiscal 2024 annual report described the company's service model as design and engineering, supply chain, manufacturing, post-production, and post-sale services delivered through a network of approximately 100 locations in approximately 30 countries. It separately described a portfolio of embedded and critical power products for data-center customers, including power shelves, battery backup units, capacitive energy-storage systems, DC/DC converters, switchgear, busway, power distribution, and modular power systems. [Flex 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637424000021/flex-20240331.htm)

That mattered because the older draft treated Flex's know-how almost as if it were an unsourced cultural asset. The filings were more concrete. Flex said it offered system architecture, user-interface and industrial design, hardware design, software integration, and design-for-excellence services; it described manufacturing services as the majority of revenue and said those services included printed circuit-board assembly, systems and subsystems assembly, testing, materials procurement, and inventory management. [Flex 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637424000021/flex-20240331.htm)

## Engineering Depth and the Product-Lifecycle Offer

The FT/Bloomberg version of the engineering story therefore rested less on slogan and more on scope. Flex's own filings repeatedly said the company helped customers design, build, deliver, and manage products across the full lifecycle.
