The 2026 filing further said the company partnered with customers across data center, healthcare, industrial, automotive, communications, and lifestyle, and that the specialized capability set included design and engineering, supply chain, manufacturing, integrated services, and a portfolio of power and cooling products. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

That lifecycle framing also showed up in current public product pages. The automotive page emphasized automotive-grade compute and power platforms plus motion and interface products. The data-center page emphasized proprietary power products, IT infrastructure solutions, liquid cooling, rack integration, and lifecycle extension through reverse logistics and refurbishment. [Flex Automotive](https://flex.com/industries/automotive), [Flex Data Center](https://flex.com/industries/data-center)

## Process Innovation as the Real Proprietary Asset

Because Flex was not a semiconductor company, the most valuable know-how sat in execution systems that were hard to mark to market. The 2026 10-K's segment note said general corporate, research and development, and administrative expenses were allocated across segments, which helps explain why the company did not present a stand-alone R&D story in the style of a pure technology vendor. But the same filing also described sustained investment in power, cooling, systems-level capabilities, advanced product-lifecycle capabilities, manufacturing technologies, and innovative processes and business methods. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

Public launches around the frozen window made that investment more legible. In October 2025, Flex said its AI infrastructure platform integrated power, cooling, compute, and services into modular designs that could cut deployment times by up to 30%. In March 2026, it unveiled NVIDIA-related reference designs that combined 800 VDC power architecture, high-density IT racks, and advanced liquid cooling, and said it was already building prefabricated modular solutions for hyperscalers at its 400,000-square-foot Dallas facility. [Flex announces new AI infrastructure platform to speed deployment by up to 30%](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-announces-new-AI-infrastructure-platform-to-speed-deployment-by-up-to-30/default.aspx), [Flex Accelerates AI Factory Deployment with NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Reference Designs](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Accelerates-AI-Factory-Deployment-with-NVIDIA-Omniverse-DSX-Reference-Designs/default.aspx)

## Complex-Systems Assembly in Practice

The better evidence for Flex's complex-systems capability came from what it publicly shipped or demonstrated. In automotive, it highlighted the Catena-X ECU exchange with BMW Group, its Jupiter Compute Platform for next-generation vehicles, and the Torc autonomous-truck platform. In healthcare, it pointed to the Merck KGaA connected autoinjector work. In data centers, it pointed to Equinix, JetCool-derived liquid-cooling products, and vertically integrated rack-and-power solutions. These were not the entire customer book, but they were enough to show that the company had public reference points in regulated and infrastructure-heavy categories where configuration control, qualification, and systems integration mattered. [Flex launches first multiregional Catena-X-based ECU data exchange with BMW Group](https://flex.com/resources/flex-launches-first-multiregional-catena-x-based-ecu-data-exchange-with-bmw-group), [Flex Wins Two 2025 PACE Awards](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-Wins-Two-2025-PACE-Awards-for-Innovation-in-Automotive-Compute-and-Power-Electronics/), [Torc collaborates with Flex on physical AI platform for autonomous trucks](https://flex.com/resources/torc-collaborates-with-flex-on-physical-ai-platform-for-autonomous-trucks), [Flex and Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, Win 2025 PDA Drug Delivery Innovation Award](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-and-Merck-KGaA-Darmstadt-Germany-Win-2025-PDA-Drug-Delivery-Innovation-Award/default.aspx), [Flex Expands Liquid Cooling Footprint at Equinix Co-Innovation Facility](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-Expands-Liquid-Cooling-Footprint-at-Equinix-Co-Innovation-Facility/default.aspx)

## The R&D Framework

The research gap in the earlier draft centered on whether Flex's modest explicit R&D disclosure meant the company was underinvesting. The filings did not support that interpretation. They supported a different one: that a significant share of Flex's engineering and development spending was embedded inside program execution and segment reporting rather than presented as a giant corporate science budget. The company said it continued to invest in targeted power, cooling, and systems capabilities, and the acquisition record around JetCool, Crown, and EP² showed that part of the development strategy was to buy specialized capabilities that could be integrated into a broader manufacturing platform. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Flex Acquires JetCool](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2024/Flex-Acquires-JetCool-to-Expand-Data-Center-and-Power-Portfolio/default.aspx), [Flex Completes Acquisition of Crown Technical Systems](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2024/Flex-Completes-Acquisition-of-Crown-Technical-Systems/default.aspx), [Flex Completes Acquisition of Electrical Power Products](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Completes-Acquisition-of-Electrical-Power-Products-EP/default.aspx)

chapters.title: EMS competition, customer concentration, supply chain, geopolitical, AI cycle
chapters.body:
## Competitive Intensity and Program Risk

The 2026 10-K left little doubt that Flex still viewed its markets as intensely competitive. The filing said the contract manufacturing market remained extremely competitive and explicitly noted that customers could cancel or delay orders, shorten commitments, or shift production volumes and locations. That mattered especially in CPI, where customer concentration was described as particularly pronounced and where a limited number of hyperscale cloud providers, colocation companies, and large enterprise data-center operators represented a substantial portion of demand. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## Customer Concentration: Less Acute Than Feared, Still Material

The earlier draft overstated concentration by naming customers the company had not named in primary-source filings. The disclosed version was narrower but still significant. In fiscal 2026, Flex's ten largest customers accounted for 45% of net sales, though no single customer exceeded 10%. That meant the company avoided the classic single-account dependency that defined some EMS histories, but it remained exposed to the decisions of a relatively small top tier. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

The risk language around CPI was more explicit than around the rest of the portfolio. Flex said hyperscale customers had substantial purchasing power and negotiating leverage, could seek favorable pricing and payment terms, and could develop in-house design, engineering, or manufacturing capabilities over time. Any decision by one or more large hyperscale customers to in-source or reallocate programs could materially affect order volumes, margins, or cash flow. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## Supply Chain and Infrastructure Constraints

The AI-linked infrastructure opportunity came with a risk stack distinct from smartphone-era EMS. Flex's 2026 risk factors said demand for cloud and power infrastructure solutions depended on continued customer investment in AI, machine learning, and high-performance computing infrastructure. They also said demand depended on customers and third-party operators securing sufficient electrical power and water within acceptable timelines and costs. Delays in utility interconnections, power-generation limits, drought, or restrictions on water use could defer deployments, reduce margins, or push out revenue. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

That was a more grounded version of the cycle-risk argument than the earlier draft's reference to public-model-efficiency newsflow. Flex's own filing did not speculate about individual model releases. It identified the relevant operational choke points directly: capital-spending volatility, power availability, water availability, facility retrofits, and mismatches between contracted volume and actual customer deployment. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## Geopolitics and Regionalization

Geography remained both asset and vulnerability. The 2026 filing showed 25% of revenue manufactured in Mexico, 19% in the U.S., 16% in China, and 11% in Malaysia. It also flagged tariffs, trade conflicts, labor constraints, and geopolitical uncertainty as continuing operating variables. For a company that sold resiliency and regional flexibility as a customer value proposition, the cost of maintaining that flexibility could itself pressure execution and margins. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## Planned Spin-Off Risk

By May 2026, Flex had added a new risk category of its own creation. The 2026 10-K devoted a separate section to planned spin-off risks, stating that the CPI separation might not be completed on the terms or timeline contemplated, if at all, and might fail to deliver the intended strategic and financial benefits. The filing pointed to execution risk, tax risk, dis-synergies, potential litigation, customer and employee retention issues, physical manufacturing separation, and governance changes, including Advaithi's move to SpinCo and Hartung's succession at Flex. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## The Real Post-Nextracker Test

The cleanest way to restate the risk chapter was this: Flex had already proven it could separate one high-growth business in Nextracker. It had not yet proved that it could separate a second one while preserving the growth, margin, and cash-generation case for what remained. That was the operational risk that sat above the rest by the frozen snapshot date.

chapters.title: Multi-segment scaling, AI data centre opportunity, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Post-Separation Baseline

By the frozen snapshot date, the relevant baseline had advanced from fiscal 2025's $25.8 billion post-Nextracker revenue floor to fiscal 2026's $27.914 billion, now split across ITS, RMS, and CPI. That did not mean the earlier post-spin reading was wrong. It meant it had become incomplete. The company had already moved from stabilization to renewed growth before the CPI separation was even executed. [Flex FY2026 results](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2026-RESULTS/default.aspx), [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## CPI and the Infrastructure Engine

The most direct forward disclosure came from the spin announcement itself. Flex said the new company would be a high-growth critical digital and electrical infrastructure business, and that SpinCo was being targeted for 65% to 75% revenue growth in fiscal 2027, accelerating to 80%+ in fiscal 2028. The company also said Flex after the spin was expected to be positioned for low-to-mid-single-digit growth, continued margin expansion, cash generation, and a robust capital-return framework. [Flex Announces Intention to Spin Off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure Segment](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Intention-to-Spin-Off-its-Cloud-and-Power-Infrastructure-Segment-into-a-New-Independent-Publicly-Traded-Company/default.aspx)

Those targets were ambitious but not detached from disclosed operating history. CPI had already grown 38% in fiscal 2026 to $6.614 billion of net sales, with a 9.2% segment margin. The product and manufacturing disclosures around that segment — up to 30% faster AI-infrastructure deployment, 600 kW to 1.8 MW liquid-cooling units, and a 400,000-square-foot Dallas data-center facility — suggested that the infrastructure business had become a real operating system rather than a simple rack-integration narrative. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Flex announces new AI infrastructure platform to speed deployment by up to 30%](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/Flex-announces-new-AI-infrastructure-platform-to-speed-deployment-by-up-to-30/default.aspx), [Flex Accelerates AI Factory Deployment with NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Reference Designs](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Accelerates-AI-Factory-Deployment-with-NVIDIA-Omniverse-DSX-Reference-Designs/default.aspx)

## RemainCo: ITS and RMS After the Carve-Out

The outlook for what stayed behind was more measured. Flex said post-spin Flex would remain organized around ITS and RMS, serving healthcare, industrial, automotive, communications, and lifestyle end markets with design, vertically integrated manufacturing, and supply-chain solutions. The company described that business as a future-ready manufacturing partner designed for speed, scale, and resilience, with more than 75 manufacturing and logistics sites across 30 countries. [Flex Announces Intention to Spin Off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure Segment](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Intention-to-Spin-Off-its-Cloud-and-Power-Infrastructure-Segment-into-a-New-Independent-Publicly-Traded-Company/default.aspx)

The internal numbers supported a cautious version of that case. ITS remained a $11.109 billion segment in fiscal 2026 despite a 2% revenue decline. RMS reached $10.191 billion, with 5% growth and 6.0% segment margin. Automotive was weaker year on year, but Industrial and Healthcare both grew. That suggested RemainCo would not be left as a hollow shell; it would still be a $20+ billion regulated-and-technology manufacturing platform. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm)

## The Scaling Variables

The fact-checked outlook rested on four variables, all disclosed or implied in primary sources.

1. **Whether CPI's growth could survive independence.** The company gave aggressive growth targets, but the 2026 10-K also warned that data-center demand depended on customer capex, power and water availability, and infrastructure readiness.
2. **Whether RemainCo could keep expanding margin without CPI inside the perimeter.** CPI had been the highest-margin segment in fiscal 2026.
3. **Whether the spin could be completed on time and on the expected tax terms.** The filing made clear that both were contingent, not guaranteed.
4. **Whether management transition would be smooth.** Advaithi was slated to move to SpinCo and Hartung to become CEO of Flex at completion. [Flex 2026 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637426000012/flex-20260331.htm), [Flex Announces Intention to Spin Off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure Segment](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2026/Flex-Announces-Intention-to-Spin-Off-its-Cloud-and-Power-Infrastructure-Segment-into-a-New-Independent-Publicly-Traded-Company/default.aspx)

## What 2026-2030 Really Meant

The pre-freeze debate had asked whether Flex could find a post-Nextracker growth engine. By May 2026 that question had already been answered in the affirmative. The new question was whether Flex was better thought of as a still-diversified advanced manufacturer with an infrastructure option, or as two companies whose valuation cases should finally be separated. The board's own actions suggested it preferred the latter answer.

## A.2 Segment Structure at the Frozen Snapshot Date

**Integrated Technology Solutions (ITS):** Communications, high-speed networking, enterprise and satellite communications systems, plus lifestyle products.

**Regulated Manufacturing Solutions (RMS):** Industrial and mission-critical automation and infrastructure, automotive compute and power electronics, and healthcare manufacturing for medical devices, drug delivery, and equipment.

**Cloud and Power Infrastructure (CPI):** Cloud and Cooling plus Power — integrated compute systems, advanced liquid cooling, and facility- and utility-level electrical infrastructure for power-dense compute workloads. financials.key_finding: Flex fiscal 2025 revenue (year ending March 2025) ~$25.8B; fiscal 2024 ~$26.4B (with substantial Nextracker contribution prior to full separation January 2024). Post-Nextracker-separation focus on Flex Agility Solutions (FAS) and Flex Reliability Solutions (FRS) with AI data centre infrastructure assembly as principal forward growth driver within FRS industrial category.
structural_observations: Advaithi-era operational restructuring delivered substantial margin expansion through 2020-2024.
Nextracker (NXT) separated via February 2023 IPO and full separation January 2024 — Nextracker was solar tracker business previously within Flex Industrial Solutions.
Post-separation, Flex segments are FAS (consumer/communications/lifestyle) and FRS (automotive/health/industrial including AI data centre).
AI data centre infrastructure assembly opportunity provides incremental growth within FRS industrial category; specific hyperscaler engagement framework continues to develop.

leadership.key_finding: Flex Ltd's executive structure reflects the strategic transformation under CEO Revathi Advaithi (since February 2019) who succeeded long-tenured CEO Mike McNamara. Advaithi joined from Eaton Corporation where she had been President and COO of Electrical Sector; the strategic mandate has been the higher-margin product and customer category emphasis, the operational efficiency improvement, the Nextracker separation completion (IPO February 2023, full separation by January 2024), and the broader strategic posture refinement. The executive team layers Advaithi's strategic continuity with CFO Paul Lundstrom (joined October 2020 from L3Harris Technologies), the segment leadership across Flex Agility Solutions and Flex Reliability Solutions, and broad operational and technology leadership. The board is chaired by John Adamovich Jr. (Lead Independent Director) and includes long-tenured directors plus more recent additions calibrated to the evolved business profile spanning consumer, automotive, health, industrial, and the emerging AI data centre infrastructure customer categories.

leadership.board_composition_observation: Flex Ltd's board pairs Lead Independent Director Adamovich (Pall Corporation CFO experience) and CEO Advaithi with directors who bring relevant operational and industry depth: Stevens for automotive-industry CFO perspective (the most directly relevant single director profile to the Flex Reliability Solutions automotive customer category), Sylvester for industrial-and-power-technology executive experience, Watkins for technology-industry CEO experience, Onetto for supply-chain-and-operations executive experience (relevant given the substantial Flex EMS supply chain context), Li for technology-industry finance experience, McSweeney for HR governance, and Tan for Asian technology-industry context relevant to the Singapore-headquartered structure. The composition reflects the company's multi-segment EMS positioning across consumer, automotive, health, industrial, and the emerging AI data centre infrastructure customer categories. The Stevens automotive-CFO experience and the Onetto supply-chain operations experience are the most strategically calibrated single director choices for the broader customer-category-relevant board governance.
